Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-0-prompt-long-0064-reverse-11", "row_sha256": "6edd86c5d1cfe7d44c92fa323291dd020845db5977028e3dbd4cf1595a9bedaf", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "i need a two-week family meal calendar for may 10 through may 23, 2027. please make it for our household, not a general sample: it’s Mara and Dev, and our kids Ivo, who is 12, and Nia, who is 8. we need dinners for every date in that range, plus lunch ideas for saturday and sunday only. leave weekday lunches and all breakfasts out. please send the finished calendar to Leonie, not Ellis. i mean Leonie is the recipient and Ellis is not; don’t address it to both of them or list Ellis as a copy. the calendar itself should be easy for the four of us to read at a glance, and it should cover those exact dates without adding a third week.

there are a few food things that matter, so keep them attached to the actual meals rather than putting them in a vague general note. Nia has a sesame allergy, so don’t use sesame or tahini in any meal, sauce, garnish, or suggested leftover. Dev is lactose intolerant, but lactose-free dairy is fine. Ivo will not eat mushrooms. Please don’t treat that as a reason to make every meal bland; we still use herbs, citrus, spices, and sauces that fit the other restrictions. Fish, poultry, and meat are all okay. We would like at least four vegetarian dinners across the two weeks, and they should be filling family meals rather than side dishes presented as dinner. Don’t make two dinners in the same week into nearly the same meal with a different name.

for the schedule, please include the date, the meal, and one short useful note about preparation or leftovers. Dinner is normally at 6:30 p.m. and we prefer food that can be on the table within 40 minutes on weeknights. Weekend dinners can take up to an hour. On Wednesday, May 12, Mara won’t be home until after 7, so make that dinner something that can wait or be reheated without turning soggy. Dev gets home late on Friday, May 14, around 7:30, and will need a portion kept warm. Thursday, May 20, Ivo has an evening school event, so dinner that night needs to be especially quick to serve; we’ll still eat at home. Don’t shift those meals to different dates or assume the family is eating out.

we have a grocery budget of about $165 for the two weeks, not counting things already in the pantry. We have rice, oats, two cans of tomatoes, two cans of chickpeas, frozen peas, tortillas, olive oil, garlic, and ordinary soy sauce. You can use those ingredients more than once, but please don’t make the whole plan depend on them. We have one oven and two stovetop burners, no slow cooker, and regular pots, pans, and a baking tray. No special equipment or specialty-shop ingredients, please. It’s fine to include a modest grocery list grouped by produce, refrigerated items, and everything else, but don’t give prices for individual items or pretend the total is exact.

we’re trying to use groceries sensibly. Reusing a cooked ingredient or an extra portion is helpful, but don’t schedule the same main dinner twice. If a dinner makes leftovers, say whether they become one of the weekend lunches or are kept for another dinner, and don’t count the same food twice. We can safely store leftovers in ordinary sealed containers in the fridge. Keep the prep notes short: we need a plan, not full recipes. A few make-ahead steps are useful if they genuinely save time, but don’t assign us a long cooking project in advance or require shopping every day.

there are some preferences too. Ivo likes tacos, baked potatoes, and mild curry, and Nia is happy with pasta, eggs, and crunchy vegetables. Those are examples of things that work, not a demand to put every favorite in the calendar. Mara likes soup for a weekend lunch, while Dev would rather have something substantial after a long walk on Saturday, so lunch ideas can differ across the weekend. We’re fine with one shared meal when it works, and no need to create separate children’s menus. We have a normal appetite range, so use sensible family portions without calculating calories or prescribing serving sizes for each person.

please make the calendar scannable rather than writing it as an essay. The bits that have to be visible are: 1) every dinner date and the two weekend lunch dates for each weekend; 2) which meals are vegetarian; and 3) the late-arrival or quick-serving notes for May 12, May 14, and May 20. A small legend is okay if you use a mark for vegetarian meals. If a grocery list is included, keep it separate from the dated calendar so it doesn’t look like another meal. Don’t include full recipes, nutrition claims, or a long explanation of how you made the plan.

one thing Dev said when we were talking about the schedule was, “I don’t mind eating leftovers, just don’t make Friday’s dinner depend on me getting home early.” That is why the May 14 portion needs to hold well until about 7:30. Please don’t turn that quote into a new rule for every Friday; it refers to this date and the practical timing above. The May 12 note is about Mara arriving later, not a request to delay dinner for everyone, and the May 20 event doesn’t mean Ivo should be left out of the plan.

we’ll print the calendar and put it on the kitchen noticeboard, so use clear date labels and wording that still makes sense on paper. Put any brief note about what can be prepared ahead in a separate final section, and only include steps that follow from the calendar. The final paragraph should be about printing and sharing the finished plan: keep the date range prominent and direct the calendar to Leonie, not Ellis. Don’t add a conclusion about whether the meals are approved, and don’t turn this into the meal calendar itself; I’m asking you to make a clear prompt for that work.", "output": "Create a clear, scannable family meal calendar for May 10–23, 2027, for Mara, Dev, and their children, Ivo (12) and Nia (8). Include a dinner for every date in that range and lunch ideas for Saturdays and Sundays only. Do not include weekday lunches, breakfasts, or dates outside the two-week period. Send the finished calendar to Leonie, not Ellis. Leonie is the recipient; do not address it to both people or list Ellis as a copy.

### Household and meal requirements

Apply the food restrictions to the meals themselves, including sauces, garnishes, and suggested leftovers:
- Nia has a sesame allergy. Do not use sesame or tahini.
- Dev is lactose intolerant; lactose-free dairy is acceptable.
- Ivo will not eat mushrooms.

Fish, poultry, and meat are acceptable. Include at least four filling vegetarian dinners across the two weeks. Keep meals varied, rather than giving the same dinner a different name, and use herbs, citrus, spices, and suitable sauces so the food is not bland. The family prefers shared meals; do not create separate children’s menus. Ivo likes tacos, baked potatoes, and mild curry; Nia likes pasta, eggs, and crunchy vegetables. Treat these as helpful preferences, not requirements to include every favorite. Mara likes soup for a weekend lunch. Dev prefers a substantial Saturday lunch after a long walk, so the weekend lunches may differ. Use sensible family portions without calculating calories or prescribing individual serving sizes.

### Schedule and timing

For each meal, show the date, the meal, and one brief, useful preparation or leftover note. Dinner is normally at 6:30 p.m. Weeknight dinners should be ready within 40 minutes; weekend dinners may take up to an hour. Account for these specific dates without moving meals or assuming anyone eats out:
1. **Wednesday, May 12:** Mara will arrive after 7 p.m. Make dinner suitable for waiting or reheating without becoming soggy. This is not a request to delay dinner for everyone.
2. **Friday, May 14:** Dev will arrive around 7:30 p.m. Keep a portion warm for him. Dev said, “I don’t mind eating leftovers, just don’t make Friday’s dinner depend on me getting home early.” This timing note applies to May 14, not every Friday.
3. **Thursday, May 20:** Ivo has an evening school event. Make dinner especially quick to serve; the family will still eat at home, and Ivo should remain included in the plan.

### Budget, ingredients, and equipment

Keep the grocery budget to about $165 for the two weeks, excluding pantry items. Available ingredients are rice, oats, two cans of tomatoes, two cans of chickpeas, frozen peas, tortillas, olive oil, garlic, and ordinary soy sauce. These may be used more than once, but the plan should not depend entirely on them. The kitchen has one oven, two stovetop burners, regular pots and pans, and a baking tray. There is no slow cooker. Avoid special equipment and specialty-shop ingredients.

Use groceries sensibly. Reusing ingredients or an extra portion is helpful, but do not schedule the same main dinner twice or count the same food twice. If dinner leftovers are planned, identify whether they become one of the weekend lunches or are kept for another dinner. Leftovers can be stored in ordinary sealed containers in the fridge. Keep preparation notes short; provide a plan, not full recipes. Include only genuinely useful make-ahead steps, without requiring a long advance cooking project or daily shopping.

### Format and final notes

Make the calendar scannable rather than essay-like. Ensure it visibly includes every dinner date, both weekend lunch dates for each weekend, which meals are vegetarian, and the special timing notes for May 12, May 14, and May 20. A small legend is fine if vegetarian meals have a mark. If you include a grocery list, place it separately from the dated calendar and group it under produce, refrigerated items, and everything else. Do not give individual item prices or present the budget total as exact. Do not include full recipes, nutrition claims, or a long explanation of the plan.

Use clear date labels and wording that will make sense when printed for the kitchen noticeboard. Put any brief, calendar-based preparation-ahead notes in a separate final section. In the final paragraph, keep the May 10–23 date range prominent and direct the finished calendar to Leonie, not Ellis. Do not add a conclusion about whether the meals are approved, and do not create the meal calendar itself; produce a prompt for that work."}]
